text: Earth spins like a top, turning once on its [[axis|axis]] about every 24 hours. At any moment, half of Earth faces [[@sun-what|the Sun]] and has day, while the other half faces away into space and has night.

As Earth turns, your part of the planet moves into the sunlight, which is sunrise, and later out of it, which is sunset. The Sun looks as if it travels across the sky, but it is really Earth that is moving.

sec.t:
Earth spins from west to east. That is why the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If you could look down on Earth from above the North Pole, you would see it turning anticlockwise.

Earth is about 40,000 km around at the [[equator|equator]]. To spin once a day, the ground there moves at about 1,670 km/h, faster than most passenger jets. In Bengaluru, near the equator, the speed is about 1,630 km/h. In New York, which is farther north, it is about 1,260 km/h, because the circle there is smaller.

We don't feel it because the spin is smooth and steady, and everything around us, including the air and the oceans, moves along with us. It is like sitting in a smooth train: you only feel the motion when it speeds up or slows down.

Because Earth spins, sunrise moves steadily westward across the planet. In India, the Sun rises in Arunachal Pradesh nearly two hours before it rises in western Gujarat. Yet the whole country uses one clock, Indian Standard Time.

The United States is much wider from east to west, so its 50 states use six main [[@time-zones|time zones]]. When it is 9 in the morning in New York, it is only 6 in Los Angeles, and still dark in Hawaii.

Earth's spin is very slowly slowing down. The Moon's pull raises [[@tides|tides]] in the oceans, and the [[friction|friction]] of all that moving water acts like a gentle brake. A day now is a few thousandths of a second longer than a day about a century and a half ago.

Over millions of years, that adds up. In 2020, scientists studied the daily growth rings in a [[fossil|fossil]] shell from about 70 million years ago. They found that a year then had about 372 days, so each day was only about 23 and a half hours long.

Almost all living things follow the [[rhythm|rhythm]] of day and night. Many flowers open in the morning and close at night. [[@owl-eyes|Owls hunt in the dark]], while crows are busy by day.

Inside your body, a natural clock, about 24 hours long, tells you when to feel awake and when to [[@sleep-why|sleep]]. Light in the morning helps set it. That is why travelling across many time zones makes people feel tired and muddled, a feeling called [[@jet-lag|jet lag]], until their body clock catches up with the Sun.

text: Nobody knows yet. No life has ever been found on Jupiter's moons. But two of them, [[@europa|Europa]] and Ganymede, almost certainly have oceans of liquid water hidden beneath thick shells of ice. Liquid water is the first thing life as we know it needs.

Europa is the favourite. Its ocean may be 60 to 150 km deep and hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans put together. It probably touches a rocky sea floor, where water and rock can react and make the kinds of chemicals that living things use for energy. Two spacecraft are now on their way to take a much closer look.

st.prompt: Europa is about five times farther from the Sun than Earth. What keeps its hidden ocean from freezing solid?

options.t: Jupiter's gravity squeezes and stretches it, making heat
Sunlight shining through the ice

st.reveal: As Europa circles Jupiter, the giant planet's gravity flexes it a little, over and over. All that bending makes heat inside the moon, enough to keep a deep ocean liquid under the ice.

n.certNote: No life has been found beyond Earth. Scientists agree that Europa and perhaps Ganymede have hidden oceans, but they disagree about how likely those oceans are to hold life.

sec.t:
In January 1610, [[@galileo|Galileo]] turned his new telescope towards [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]]. Next to it he saw three, then four, small points of light. Night after night they shifted from one side of the planet to the other. He realised they were moons circling Jupiter.

That was a shock. Many people at the time believed everything in the sky circled Earth. Here was proof that some things circled something else. Those four moons, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, are still called the Galilean moons. Jupiter is now known to have more than 90 moons, but most are only a few kilometres across.

Io is the most volcanic place in the [[solar-system|solar system]], with hundreds of active [[@volcano|volcanoes]]. Europa is about the size of our Moon and covered in ice scored with long reddish-brown cracks. Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, wider than the planet [[@mercury-planet|Mercury]], and the only moon known to make its own magnetic field. Callisto is the most heavily cratered and may also have a deep ocean.

What heats them is Jupiter itself. Its powerful [[gravity|gravity]] squeezes these moons as they [[orbit|orbit]], a bit like a hand squeezing a rubber ball. The flexing makes heat. On Io that heat melts rock. On Europa it seems to be just enough to keep water liquid under the ice, the same way [[@why-ice-floats|ice floats]] as a lid on a frozen pond.

Europe's JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer) launched in April 2023 and is due to reach Jupiter in 2031. It will study Europa, Callisto and especially Ganymede, which it will eventually orbit.

NASA's Europa Clipper launched in October 2024 and should arrive in 2030. It will fly past Europa about 50 times, measuring how thick the ice is and tasting any gases or dust thrown off the surface. It cannot dig into the ocean or find living things directly. What it can do is tell us whether Europa has everything life would need.

The Galileo spacecraft, which studied Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, helped prove Europa's ocean was there. When its fuel ran low, controllers steered it into Jupiter's clouds so that it could never crash on Europa and bring Earth [[microbe|microbes]] along. Whatever lives on Europa, if anything does, scientists want to find it untouched.

text: The Voyager Golden Record is a message in a bottle for the stars. In 1977, NASA launched two spacecraft, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, to fly past Jupiter, Saturn and beyond. Bolted to the side of each is a 30 cm record made of copper and covered in gold.

The record holds greetings in 55 languages, music from around the world, sounds of Earth and 115 pictures. It also carries instructions, cut into its cover, showing how to play it. Both Voyagers are now outside the bubble of the Sun's wind, travelling between the stars. If anyone ever finds one, the record is our hello.

st.prompt: How did NASA store 115 pictures on the Golden Record?

options.t: As sound signals that can be turned back into pictures
As tiny paintings glued to the record
As photos printed on the cover

st.reveal: The pictures were turned into signals and pressed into the grooves, like music. A listener who follows the instructions on the cover can rebuild them line by line, a bit like an old television.

d.try: Make your own golden record list. Choose five sounds, five pictures and one song that you think best explain life on Earth to someone who has never been here. Compare your list with a friend's and argue about what made the cut.
myth: The Golden Record was sent to a specific alien planet.
The Voyagers are not aimed at any planet. They will drift between the stars for millions of years, and the record will only be found if someone happens to come across it.

sec.t:
NASA gave the job to a small committee led by the [[astronomer|astronomer]] Carl Sagan. They had about six weeks to decide what should represent all of humanity. They argued over every choice.

They picked pictures of DNA, a mother feeding a baby, a supermarket, a page from a book and the Taj Mahal. They chose sounds like rain, wind, footsteps, a kiss, a laughing child, a train, a dog barking and a heartbeat. The spoken greetings range from ancient Sumerian to modern languages. Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi, Telugu, Kannada, Punjabi and Urdu are all there.

sec.h: How to play a record with no record player
sec.t:
The aliens would need to build their own player. The record came with a needle and cartridge, and its cover shows, in drawings and [[binary|binary]] code, how to place the needle and how fast to spin it. It even shows how to turn the signals into pictures.

To say where we live, the cover has a map of 14 pulsars, stars that flash like lighthouses at precise speeds. From the pattern, someone clever could work out the position of our Sun. There is also a tiny dab of uranium on the cover. It decays at a known rate, so it acts like a clock showing how long ago the record left.

sec.h: A message that will outlast us
sec.t:
The record is made to last. Out between the stars there is no air, no rust and very little dust, so it could survive for hundreds of millions of years, maybe a billion. The Earth's continents will have shifted shape long before it wears out.

In November 2026, Voyager 1 is set to reach one light-day from Earth, about 25.9 billion km. Signals from NASA, travelling at the speed of light, will take about a full day to reach it. Even so, it will not pass close to another star for about 40,000 years, and space is so empty that nobody may ever find the record. Some scientists say that is fine. Making it forced humans to ask what we would want strangers to know about us.

Voyager 1 is still sending faint signals home with a radio of about 22 watts, roughly as much power as a fridge light bulb. How a nearly 50-year-old machine manages that, and what it has discovered, is the story of the [[@voyager|Voyager probes]]. How far 40,000 years of travel really is becomes clearer once you understand [[@light-years|light-years]]. And whether anyone is out there to listen is one of the biggest questions in science, explored in [[@alien-life|alien life]].

text: Bar-headed geese spend the winter on lakes and rivers in India. Each spring they fly north over the Himalayas to breed in Tibet, Mongolia and Central Asia, then return in autumn.

Up there the air is thin. At 5 km, each breath holds only about half the oxygen it would at sea level, and many people get altitude sickness. The geese cope because their blood grabs oxygen unusually well, and their lungs, hearts and flight [[@muscles|muscles]] are built to make the most of every breath. They usually fly through mountain passes 5 to 6 km high, following the shape of the land instead of staying high all the time.

sec.t:
In 2015, scientists fitted geese with small devices that recorded their heartbeat, height and wingbeats. They expected the birds to climb high and stay there. Instead, the geese rose and fell with the ground below, like a roller coaster.

Climbing costs a lot of energy, but flying in thin air costs even more, because each wingbeat has less air to push against. Hugging the slopes kept them in denser air. The highest any tracked goose went was about 7.3 km. Some crossings took about seven or eight hours from the plains to the Tibetan plateau.

Bar-headed geese reach India around October and leave again by March or April. They are named for the two dark bars across the back of their white heads. Big flocks winter at Pong Dam lake in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], and smaller groups spread south across the country to lakes and rivers in states such as Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

In winter they rest on water by day and often graze at night on grasses and young crops in fields nearby, which does not always please farmers. Like many geese, pairs usually stay together for years and travel as families, with the young birds learning the route from their parents. So when you see a flock on a lake near you, some of those birds may have crossed the Himalayas many times.

sec.h: An old journey over young mountains
sec.t:
The [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas]] rose as India pushed into Asia, and they are still rising by a few millimetres a year. The geese may have been making this crossing for a very long time, but nobody knows exactly how long.

[[@mountaineering|Climbers on Everest]] need weeks to get used to the height, and most carry oxygen tanks near the top. When Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary reached the summit in 1953 ([[@everest-first|read their story]]), they breathed bottled oxygen. A goose makes a similar climb in one day, flapping all the way. In winter you can see these geese, with two dark bars on their white heads, on lakes from Himachal Pradesh down to Karnataka. Their journey is one of many described in [[@migration|bird migration]].

text: The deepest known point in the ocean is the Challenger Deep, at the southern end of the Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean. It lies about 11 km below the waves. If you dropped [[@mountains-tallest|Mount Everest]] in, its peak would still be about 2 km underwater.

At the bottom it is pitch dark and close to freezing. The water [[pressure|pressure]] is over 1,000 times what you feel at the beach. That is like having about a tonne pressing on every patch of skin the size of your fingernail.
And yet things live there. Pale, shrimp-like creatures scuttle over the mud, eating anything that drifts down from the sunlit sea far above.

spots: The Challenger Deep is about 11 km deep. Everest is 8.85 km tall. It would be covered with 2 km to spare!
In 1960, two explorers reached the bottom in a submarine called Trieste. More have gone since.
Pale, jelly-like fish live deeper than 8 km. They're the deepest fish ever filmed.
Amphipods scurry around at the very bottom, eating anything that sinks.

myth: Nothing can live at the bottom of the deepest ocean.
Every visit to the Challenger Deep has found life. Shrimp-like amphipods, sea cucumbers, giant single-celled creatures and many kinds of microbes all live there.

sec.t:
The Mariana Trench is a long, curved valley in the ocean floor, about 2,500 km long. It formed where one huge slab of [[@earth-layers-crust|Earth's crust]], the Pacific plate, slides down underneath another. This kind of grinding edge also causes [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]] and builds chains of volcanic islands.

The Challenger Deep is named after a British ship, HMS Challenger, which measured the trench in 1875 by lowering a weighted rope. Later ships used echoes of sound, and found an even deeper spot. Scientists still argue about the exact depth by a few metres, because measuring through 11 km of water is hard.

On 23 January 1960, two explorers, Jacques Piccard from Switzerland and Don Walsh from the US Navy, squeezed into a steel ball under a craft called the Trieste. Partway down, they heard a loud crack. One of the outer windows had split, but they kept going.

After nearly five hours they touched the bottom. Their landing stirred up a cloud of silt, so they could see very little. They stayed about 20 minutes, then rose back up.

Nobody returned for 52 years. In 2012 the [[@hollywood|film-maker]] James Cameron dived alone. Since 2019, a new [[@ocean-explorers|submersible]] has made many trips. In 2020 it carried Kathryn Sullivan, the first American woman to walk in space, making her the first person to do both.

{{story:himalaya-form}}

Deep-sea creatures have soft bodies with no air spaces to crush. Amphipods, cousins of the sandhoppers on a beach, are the most common visitors to bait left at the bottom. Some can even digest bits of sunken wood.

Fish can't quite reach the very bottom. Scientists think that below about 8,200 to 8,400 m, the chemistry inside a fish's body stops working properly. In 2023, a team filmed a small snailfish at about 8,300 m in a trench off Japan, the deepest fish ever seen.

Even here, people have left a mark. A plastic bag was spotted at almost 11 km deep, and [[@ocean-plastic|ocean plastic]] has been found in the guts of animals living in the trench.

The Indian Ocean's deepest point is in the Java Trench, south of Indonesia, at about 7 km. India is building its own crewed submersible, [[@ocean-exploration-india|Matsya-6000]], as part of its Deep Ocean Mission. It is designed to carry three people to 6 km below the surface.

Scientists at the National Institute of Ocean Technology in Chennai have been testing it. Its job will be to study the deep seabed and its life. If it succeeds, India will join the small group of countries that can send people into the [[@ocean-zones|deepest zones]] of the sea. The bottom of the ocean is closer to us than the Moon, yet we have still seen only a sliver of it.

text: In seahorses, the female makes the eggs, but the male carries them. He has a pouch on his belly, a bit like a kangaroo's. During courtship, the female places her eggs into the male's pouch, and he fertilises them there. For the next two to four weeks, he is pregnant.

Inside the pouch, the father keeps the eggs safe, controls the saltiness of the water around them and helps supply oxygen. When the babies are ready, he pumps and twists until they shoot out of the pouch in little clouds. A single birth can release from a few babies to more than a thousand, depending on the kind of seahorse. They are on their own from the moment they are born.

Its curly tail, pushing like a spring

st.reveal: A seahorse is pushed along by its small back fin, which flutters dozens of times a second. Tiny fins near its head help it steer. It is one of the slowest swimmers in the sea.

Seahorses are bony fish. They breathe with gills, have fins and a swim bladder, and are closely related to pipefish. They just look very different from most fish.

sec.t:
Nobody knows for certain why male seahorses became the pregnant ones. One popular idea is speed. While the male carries one batch of babies, the female can start making the next batch of eggs. When he gives birth, she may be ready again almost straight away. Working as a team, the pair can produce more young in a season.

Another idea is that carrying the eggs lets the male be sure the babies are his own. Scientists are still testing these ideas, and the answer may involve both. Seahorses are not the only fish with caring dads. In their relatives, the seadragons, the male carries the eggs stuck to the underside of his tail. Among birds, emperor [[@penguins-cold|penguin]] fathers balance an egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter.

Many seahorses form pairs that stay together for at least a breeding season. In some kinds, the partners meet every morning for a short greeting dance. They change colour, circle each other and sometimes hold tails. Scientists think this daily dance keeps the pair in step, so they are ready to breed at the same time.

This partnership matters because seahorses live in small home areas and move slowly. Finding a new mate can be hard, so keeping the same one makes sense.

Seahorses live in shallow coastal water around the world, in seagrass beds, [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] and the roots of [[@mangroves|mangroves]]. In India they are found in places such as the Gulf of Mannar and Palk Bay, the shallow waters between Tamil Nadu and [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]].

Millions of seahorses are taken from the sea each year, many caught by accident in nets meant for shrimp. Dried seahorses are also used in traditional medicines in parts of Asia, and some are sold as souvenirs or aquarium pets. Since 2004, international trade in all seahorses has been controlled under a global agreement called CITES. India gave seahorses its highest legal protection in 2001.

text: A caterpillar becomes a butterfly through a complete change of body called [[metamorphosis|metamorphosis]]. It happens in four stages: egg, caterpillar, [[pupa|pupa]] and adult.

The caterpillar's job is to eat and grow. When it is big enough, it hangs up and sheds its skin one last time, revealing a hard case called a chrysalis, or pupa. Inside, its body is taken apart. Special juices break down much of the caterpillar into a soupy mush.

Then groups of cells that have been waiting quietly since the caterpillar was in its egg spring into action. They use the mush as building material to make wings, long legs, big eyes and a coiled drinking tube. Days or weeks later, a butterfly climbs out.

st.prompt: How does a mother butterfly check that a leaf is the right food for her caterpillars?

options.t: She smells it with her wings
She tastes it with her feet
She watches where other butterflies lay

st.reveal: Butterflies have taste sensors on their feet. A female lands on a leaf and drums on it, scratching the surface to release its juices. If it tastes right, she lays her eggs there, because each kind of caterpillar can only eat certain plants.

d.try: With an adult, look under the leaves of a lemon, curry leaf or other citrus plant. You may find small caterpillars that look like bird droppings, the young of the lime butterfly. Visit each day without moving them, and draw what you see. If you're lucky, you'll spot a chrysalis.

A cocoon is a silk case that many moth caterpillars spin around themselves. Butterflies make a chrysalis instead, a hard case that forms from the caterpillar's own skin.

sec.t:
A caterpillar does almost nothing but eat. Some kinds grow to more than a thousand times their weight at hatching in just two or three weeks. If a human baby grew that fast, it would end up as heavy as an elephant.

Its skin can't stretch that much, so the caterpillar sheds it several times, wriggling out of the old skin with a new, looser one underneath. Each caterpillar can only eat certain plants. That is why the mother chooses so carefully where to lay her eggs.

Many caterpillars protect themselves with tricks. Some look like bird droppings. Others have fake eye spots, spines or bright colours that warn birds they taste bad.

When the butterfly first climbs out, its wings are crumpled and soft. It pumps blood into the [[vein|veins]] to stretch them out, then waits for them to dry and harden before it can fly.

Butterfly wings are covered in thousands of tiny overlapping scales, like roof tiles. That is the "dust" that rubs off on your fingers. Some colours come from [[pigment|pigments]]. Others, like the shimmering blue of some swallowtails, come from the way tiny ridges on the scales bounce light around. A butterfly's two wings are almost perfect mirror images, a good example of [[@symmetry|symmetry]].

India has about 1,300 kinds of butterfly. In 2015, Maharashtra became the first state to choose a state butterfly, the blue Mormon, a big black swallowtail with glowing blue patches. Karnataka chose the Southern birdwing, one of India's largest butterflies, whose wings can stretch about as wide as an adult's hand.

After [[@monsoon|the monsoon]], you may see groups of butterflies sipping at damp mud. This is called puddling. They are drinking salts and minerals that the males need. In the USA, the monarch butterfly makes one of the longest insect journeys on Earth, flying thousands of kilometres to Mexico, as told in [[@monarch-migration|monarch migration]].

Moths go through the same change. Many moth caterpillars spin a silk case called a [[cocoon|cocoon]] around themselves. One of them, the silkworm, spins the thread used to weave [[@silk|silk]] sarees.

text: A ghazal (said "guh-zul") is a kind of poem built from [[couplet|couplets]], pairs of lines called *sher*. Each couplet is complete in itself, like a tiny poem. What ties them together is sound. Every couplet ends with the same word or phrase, called the radif, and just before it comes a rhyme called the qafia.

The form began in Arabic, flowered in Persian, and came to India with poets and kings who spoke Persian. In [[@urdu|Urdu]] it became one of the best-loved kinds of poetry. Sung to music, the ghazal grew into a style that fills concert halls from Lucknow to Lahore, and film songs too.

st.reveal: The final couplet, the maqta, traditionally includes the poet's takhallus, or pen name. Ghalib, for example, often speaks to himself by name in his last lines, as if a friend were teasing him.

sec.t:
A ghazal usually has five to fifteen couplets. The first one, the matla, sets the pattern: both of its lines end with the radif. After that, only the second line of each couplet does. The last couplet, the maqta, often contains the poet's pen name.

Say the radif is "by the sea". One couplet might end "I dropped my key by the sea", the next "Nani sang to me by the sea". The rhyming words, key and me, change each time. The radif stays put.

Because each couplet stands alone, a ghazal can jump from love to faith to a joke about the weather. Listeners wait for the radif to come back, and enjoy guessing how the poet will reach it this time. At a gathering called a mushaira, the crowd often shouts "wah wah" and asks to hear a good couplet again.

Long before Ghalib, the Persian poets Rumi and Hafez wrote ghazals that are still recited in Iran. Persian was the language of courts across northern India for centuries, so the form travelled. Amir Khusrau, a poet and musician in Delhi around 1300, wrote ghazals in Persian and mixed in the local tongue.

By the 1600s, poets in the Deccan were writing ghazals in an early form of Urdu. Later, Mir Taqi Mir, Daagh, Faiz Ahmad Faiz and many others kept the form alive. Today ghazals are written in Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Punjabi, Bengali and more.

Singing a ghazal is gentler than the roaring [[@qawwali|qawwali]]. The singer lingers over the words, so the audience can taste them. Begum Akhtar, from Faizabad, was called Mallika-e-Ghazal, the queen of ghazal, in the mid-1900s. Mehdi Hassan and Ghulam Ali became stars in Pakistan and India alike.

In the 1970s and 80s, Jagjit Singh brought ghazals to millions of new listeners with simple tunes, guitars and a soft voice. Many Hindi [[@film-songs|film songs]] borrow the form, with a repeated phrase at the end of each verse.

The Kashmiri-American poet Agha Shahid Ali, who taught at universities in the USA, wanted English speakers to write "real ghazals" that followed the old rules. In 2000 he edited a collection of them by American poets. His own ghazals mix memories of [[@kashmir|Kashmir]] with life in America. So a form that began in Arabian deserts now turns up in poetry classes in Ohio and Bengaluru.

text: India's mathematical story didn't end with Aryabhata or [[@ramanujan|Ramanujan]]. In the last hundred years, Indian mathematicians have built new fields, solved old puzzles and won the world's top prizes. Some worked in India, at places like the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata or the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai. Others did their work in the USA, the UK or Australia.
Here are a few of them, from a statistician who helped plan India's [[economy|economy]] to a schoolteacher with a magic number.

st.reveal: 5432 minus 2345 is 3087. Then 8730 minus 0378 is 8352, and 8532 minus 2358 is 6174. From 6174, you get 7641 minus 1467, which is 6174 again. D. R. Kaprekar discovered this in 1949.

sec.t:
Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis was a physicist who fell in love with [[statistics|statistics]], the maths of data. In 1931, he founded the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata. He invented a way of measuring how different two groups are, now called the Mahalanobis distance, which is used in fields from medicine to [[@face-recognition|face recognition]]. It helps a computer decide whether a new measurement looks more like one group or another.

He also designed huge sample surveys to understand how Indians lived, worked and spent money. The National Sample Survey, which he helped begin in 1950, still runs today. His student C. R. Rao became one of the most important statisticians in the world and, aged 102, received the International Prize in Statistics in 2023.

Not every mathematician works at a university. Dattatreya Ramchandra Kaprekar taught at a school in Devlali, near Nashik, and played with numbers in his spare time. In 1949 he found that almost any four-digit number, put through a simple routine of rearranging and subtracting, ends up at 6174. It is now called Kaprekar's constant.

He found many other number patterns too. For years, professional mathematicians ignored him, and he had to publish many of his ideas in small journals or at his own cost. Today, puzzle books and maths clubs all over the world use his discoveries.

Harish-Chandra, born in Kanpur in 1923, did deep work on [[symmetry|symmetry]] in mathematics at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. A research institute in Prayagraj is named after him.

S. R. Srinivasa Varadhan, who grew up in Chennai, won the Abel Prize in 2007 for his work on [[@probability|probability]], the maths of chance. Manjul Bhargava, an American mathematician whose family comes from India, won the Fields Medal in 2014. He has said that Sanskrit poetry and tabla [[rhythm|rhythms]] helped spark his love of patterns. Akshay Venkatesh, born in New Delhi and raised in Australia, won the Fields Medal in 2018.

The story continues. Neena Gupta of the Indian Statistical Institute solved a famous problem in algebra and won the Ramanujan Prize for young mathematicians in 2021. Raman Parimala, known for her work in algebra, has been honoured around the world.

Each year, Indian students also compete in the International [[@maths-olympiad|Mathematical Olympiad]], and many bring back medals. Some of them may be the names in an article like this one, fifty years from now.

text: After a trillion comes a quadrillion, then a quintillion, sextillion, septillion, octillion, nonillion and decillion. Each one is a thousand times bigger than the one before.

A million has 6 zeros. A billion has 9, a trillion 12, a quadrillion 15 and a quintillion 18. The names follow Latin counting words: *quadr-* means four, *quint-* five, *sext-* six, *dec-* ten. So you can keep going with names like vigintillion, which has 63 zeros. In India, the same amounts can also be named in [[@lakh-crore|lakh and crore]], which group zeros differently.

options.t: Nearly 32 years

st.reveal: There are about 31.5 million seconds in a year, so a billion seconds takes almost 32 years to tick by. A million seconds is under two weeks. The jump from million to billion is much bigger than it sounds.

myth: A billion means the same number in every country.

In the past, Britain and much of Europe used "billion" to mean a million million, which has 12 zeros. Britain switched to the American billion of 9 zeros in 1974, but in French, German and Spanish the word that sounds like "billion" still means 12 zeros.

sec.t:
Most English speakers today use what mathematicians call the short scale. Every new name means "multiply by a thousand". It matches the way we put commas in numbers: 1,000,000,000 for a billion, with three zeros between each comma.

Mathematicians usually skip the names and use [[@exponents|powers of ten]]. A quintillion is written 10¹⁸, which means 1 with 18 zeros after it. It's shorter, harder to misread and works the same in every language.

To feel the size of these jumps, think about time. A million seconds is about 11 and a half days. A billion seconds is nearly 32 years. A trillion seconds is about 31,700 years, which takes you back to the last Ice Age, long before anyone built a city.

For centuries Britain and much of Europe used the long scale, in which each new name meant a million times bigger. A billion was a million million, which has 12 zeros. Britain officially switched to the American billion in 1974.

Many European languages still use the long scale. In French, a *milliard* has 9 zeros and a *billion* has 12. Translators and news reporters have to be careful, or a country's budget can come out a thousand times too big. Scientists avoid the problem by writing powers of ten, which mean the same thing in every country.

Indian newspapers face a similar puzzle every day. The same sum might be reported as 10 crore rupees in one story and 100 million rupees in another. Both are correct.

sec.h: The googol and its giant cousin
sec.t:
In 1920, the American mathematician Edward Kasner asked his nine-year-old nephew, Milton Sirotta, to make up a name for 1 followed by 100 zeros. Milton said "googol". He also suggested an even bigger number, the googolplex: 1 followed by a googol of zeros. Kasner put both in a book in 1940.

A googol is far more than the number of [[atom|atoms]] scientists estimate are in the whole visible universe, which is around 10⁸⁰. A googolplex is so big you could never write it out, because there isn't enough space in the universe for all the zeros. Decades later, the founders of [[@search-engines|Google]] named their company after the googol, spelling it differently.

Scientists also need names for giant measured amounts. In 2022, the international body that runs the metric system added two new prefixes: *ronna*, for 27 zeros, and *quetta*, for 30. The mass of the Earth is about 6 ronnagrams. Even so, all these numbers are still finite. Keep adding zeros forever and you never reach [[@infinity|infinity]], which isn't really a number at all.

text: Place value means that a digit's worth depends on where it sits in a number. In 444, all three digits are the same, but they mean different things. The one on the right is 4 ones. The middle one is 4 tens, or 40. The left one is 4 hundreds, or 400. Together they make 400 + 40 + 4.

Each place is worth ten times the place to its right. That's why we call it a base-10 system. With just ten digits, 0 to 9, and the rule of places, you can write any number at all, from your age to the number of stars in the [[galaxy|galaxy]].

st.prompt: In the number 5,372, how much is the 3 worth?
st.reveal: The 3 sits in the hundreds place, so it means 3 hundreds, or 300. Reading from the right, the places are ones, tens, hundreds and thousands, each ten times bigger than the one before.

sec.t:
Not every number system works this way. In Roman numerals, X always means 10, wherever it appears. To write 2026 the Romans wrote MMXXVI: two thousands, two tens, a five and a one. Big numbers need long strings of letters, and doing a sum like 3,847 × 26 is very difficult.

Many ancient peoples counted with marks, knots or pebbles. Pebbles in Latin are *calculi*, which is where the word "calculate" comes from. To do sums, merchants used counting boards or an [[@abacus|abacus]], moving beads up and down in rows. Each row stood for ones, tens or hundreds. In a way, the abacus used place value long before people wrote it down.

Around 4,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia used place value too, but in base 60. Each place was worth sixty times the place to its right. Sixty can be split evenly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths, which made dividing easy.

We still live with their system. There are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour, which is how [[@clocks|clocks]] count. A circle has 360 degrees. When a clock reads 2:45, it's really a base-60 number: 2 hours and 45 sixtieths of an hour.

Place value works the same everywhere, but people group the digits differently when they write big numbers. In India, after the first three digits, commas come every two places: 1,00,000 is one lakh and 1,00,00,000 is one crore. In the USA and much of the world, commas come every three places: 100,000 and 10,000,000.

Both are correct. One [[@lakh-crore|lakh]] and a hundred thousand are exactly the same amount, with the commas in different places. The digits and their places don't change at all.

Place value doesn't have to use ten. The Maya of Central America used base 20, possibly from counting on fingers and toes, and also had a symbol for zero. Computers use base 2, called [[@binary-code|binary]], with only 0 and 1. In [[binary|binary]], each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. So 101 in binary means 4 + 0 + 1, which is 5.

A car's odometer is a good picture of place value. When the ones wheel rolls past 9 back to 0, it nudges the tens wheel forward by one. Every number system with places works this way, whatever its base.

text: A tangram is a puzzle made from a square cut into seven pieces, called tans. There are two large triangles, one medium triangle, two small triangles, one square and one parallelogram, a slanted rectangle.

The game is to use all seven pieces, laid flat and not overlapping, to make a shape. Usually you are shown only the outline, a solid silhouette of a cat, a teapot or a dancing person, and you have to work out where each piece goes. The puzzle comes from China, where it is called qiqiaoban, "seven boards of skill". It spread around the world about 200 years ago and is still used in classrooms to teach [[@shapes-angles|shapes]].

st.prompt: If each small triangle in a tangram set covers 1 unit of area, how many units does the whole square cover?
st.reveal: The two small triangles are 1 each. The medium triangle, the square and the parallelogram are 2 each. The two large triangles are 4 each. Add them up and you get 16.

Try to make a cat, a house and a boat. Then put the square back together, which is harder than it sounds.
myth: Tangrams are 4,000 years old and were invented by a Chinese man named Tan.

This story was made up as a joke by the American puzzle writer Sam Loyd in 1903. The earliest known tangram books are from China around 1813, and the puzzle is probably not much older than the late 1700s.

sec.t:
The pieces fit together in a neat way. Take the small triangle as one unit. The square, the parallelogram and the medium triangle each cover two units. Each large triangle covers four. All seven together make 16.

The angles fit too. Every corner on every piece is 45, 90 or 135 degrees. That is why the pieces slide together so neatly, and why so many shapes can be made. People have published thousands of tangram figures, and you can always invent new ones.

The earliest books of tangram puzzles we know of were printed in China around 1813. The game probably appeared there not long before, in the late 1700s.

Sailors and traders soon carried it abroad. Around 1817, tangrams became a craze in Europe and the United States. Books of puzzles sold quickly, and people played at parties. A story says that [[@napoleon|Napoleon]], sent into exile on the island of St Helena, passed the time with a tangram set. Historians aren't sure it's true, but sets from that period do survive.

The puzzle may have grown out of older [[@ancient-china|Chinese]] ideas, such as sets of banquet tables that could be pushed together in different patterns. In China itself, tangram books kept being printed all through the 1800s.

{{story:board-games}}

In 1903 Sam Loyd, a famous American puzzle maker, published a book about tangrams. In it he claimed the puzzle was 4,000 years old, invented by a god named Tan, and that ancient books described seven sets of a thousand puzzles each.

None of it was true. Loyd was known for playful tricks, and he probably expected readers to see the joke. Many didn't. His story was repeated in books and newspapers for decades. Even now, you may read that tangrams are thousands of years old. The real story is younger, though no less interesting.

Some tangram pictures look like magic. The English puzzle writer Henry Dudeney showed two figures of a man that look almost exactly the same. Both use all seven pieces. Yet one man has a foot and the other doesn't.

The trick is that the bodies are slightly different shapes. The area of the missing foot has been spread around the rest of the figure, so thinly you hardly notice. This kind of puzzle is a visual [[@paradoxes|paradox]], and it teaches you to check the area instead of trusting your eyes.

A convex shape is one with no dents. A rubber band stretched around it would touch every edge. In 1942, two mathematicians from China, Wang Fu Traing and Hsiung Chuan-Chih, asked how many convex shapes the seven tans can make. They proved the answer is exactly 13. These include a square, a rectangle, a triangle and several kinds of five- and six-sided shapes.

Tangrams are now used in schools from Delhi to Detroit. They help children learn about area, angles and fractions with their hands. And for people of any age, they offer a quiet challenge: seven pieces, one outline, no peeking at the answer.

text: Yes, computers can write music, and they have done it for almost 70 years. Today's AI programs can produce a full song with drums, melody, lyrics and a singing voice in less than a minute. All you type is a short description, like "a happy song about [[monsoon|monsoon]] rain".

They do it by studying enormous amounts of recorded music and learning its patterns: which notes sound good together, how a chorus repeats, what a drum beat in hip hop sounds like. Then they generate new music that follows those patterns.
What they cannot do, as far as anyone can tell, is feel anything about it. Whether that makes them real composers is one of the big arguments of the 2020s.

st.prompt: Modern AI music programs learn by studying huge amounts of music. What are they mostly learning to do?

options.t: Guess what sound should come next
Memorise and play back whole songs

st.reveal: Like a phone keyboard guessing your next word, music AI learns which notes, beats and sounds tend to follow each other. It then builds new music one tiny step at a time. It has no feelings about what it makes.

sec.h: Music with dice and early machines
sec.t:
The idea is older than computers. In 1843, the mathematician [[@ada-lovelace|Ada Lovelace]] wrote that a calculating engine might "compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity". Nobody had built such a machine yet.

Even earlier, in the 1700s, people in Europe played "musical dice games". You rolled dice to choose which short bar of music came next, stitching together a new minuet each time. One of these games was published under [[@mozart|Mozart's]] name in 1792, though experts are not certain he wrote it.

In 1957, two scientists at the University of Illinois, Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson, used a room-sized computer called ILLIAC I to write a piece for string quartet. They called it the Illiac Suite. The computer picked notes at random, then threw out any that broke rules of harmony. It was clunky, but it was a start. The music sounds a bit stiff today, yet it was performed by real string players and recorded, and people argued about whether a machine should be allowed to compose at all. That argument has never really stopped.

{{story:maths-music}}

sec.h: How today's AI makes a song
sec.t:
Modern music AI works a bit like the [[@large-language-models|chatbots]] that write sentences. A chatbot learns which word usually comes next. A music model learns which tiny slice of sound usually comes next, thousands of times every second.

To learn, it is fed huge collections of songs. Over time it picks up the shape of a ballad, the swing of jazz and the growl of rock guitar. Ask it for "a lullaby with a flute", and it builds one from scratch, one small step at a time.

[[@maths-music|Music]] is full of maths, such as repeating [[rhythm|rhythms]] and note frequencies in neat ratios. That makes it a good puzzle for a pattern-learning machine.

The songs used to train these programs were written and recorded by real people, and most were never asked. In 2024, major record companies took two well-known AI song makers to court in the USA, saying they had copied music without permission. In late 2025, some of these companies agreed to settle and work on licensed versions instead, while other cases carried on.

Governments are still deciding the rules. The US Copyright Office has said that music made entirely by AI, with no real human creative choices, cannot be protected by copyright.

Many musicians use AI as a tool. It can clean up old recordings, separate a singer's voice from the instruments, or suggest a chord when a songwriter is stuck. In 2023, technology like this helped pull John Lennon's voice out of an old, muffled tape, so the Beatles could finish one last song.

In India, composers have experimented with AI to recreate the voices of singers who have died, with their families' permission, which some listeners found moving and others found uneasy. That same trick of copying a voice is now one of the most powerful and worrying things AI can do with sound.

text: You get spam because sending it is almost free, and a tiny number of people fall for it. If a spammer sends 10 million emails and only a handful of people buy a fake product, click a bad link or hand over a password, the spammer can still profit.

Spam is unwanted email sent in bulk to huge numbers of people. Some is just annoying advertising. Some is dangerous: messages pretending to be from your bank, a delivery company or even a friend, trying to steal passwords or money. That kind is called phishing.
By most counts in the mid-2020s, close to half of all email sent worldwide is spam. Most of it never reaches you, because filters catch it first.

st.prompt: A spammer sends 10 million emails, and only 1 person in a million buys what they are selling. Why might the spammer still make money?

Every email pays the spammer a small fee

st.reveal: Ten sales from 10 million emails sounds tiny. But sending email in bulk costs so little, especially from hijacked computers, that a handful of buyers can still mean a profit. That's why spam never stops.

sec.t:
On 3 May 1978, a marketing manager at an American computer company called DEC sent a message to about 400 people on ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet. It invited them to see a demonstration of new computers.

Many people were furious. ARPANET was meant for research, not adverts. But the company reportedly sold some computers as a result. A lesson was learned that has never gone away: bulk messages annoy people but sometimes pay.

Spam works because of very small chances multiplied by very large numbers. In 2008, researchers in California quietly took over part of a real spam network to study it. They found that out of about 350 million emails advertising fake medicine, only 28 led to a sale, about 1 in 12.5 million.

That sounds hopeless. But big spam networks were sending billions of messages a day, so those tiny [[@probability|chances]] could still add up to real money.

Much spam is sent from ordinary home computers that have been secretly taken over by viruses. Their owners usually have no idea. Thousands of these hijacked computers working together are called a botnet.

Email services fight spam with filters that sort each message as it arrives. Early filters looked for words like "free money". Spammers simply misspelled them.

So in the early 2000s, programmers built filters that learn. They study millions of emails people have marked as spam or not spam, and work out patterns. The filters look at the words, the sender's address, the links, and whether thousands of identical messages are arriving at once. Each time you press "report spam", you help train them. These smart [[@algorithms|algorithms]] now catch the vast majority of spam before it lands in your inbox.

Email is just one front. In India, phones get waves of unwanted calls and text messages too, and the telecom regulator runs a Do Not Disturb list to block marketing calls.

A few habits protect you. Don't click links or open attachments in messages you were not expecting, even if they look official. Real banks never ask for your password or PIN by email or text. If in doubt, ask an adult to check, or go to the company's website directly.

Messages that say "act now" or "you have won" are classic warning signs. Spammers try to make you hurry, because a person who stops to think is much harder to fool. That rush-and-panic trick is now being made even more convincing with AI, which can write polished fake messages and even copy the [[@tech-voice-cloning|voices]] of people you know.

text: UPI stands for Unified Payments Interface. It is a set of rules and computer systems that lets any bank in India talk to any other bank instantly. When you scan a shop's QR code and type your secret PIN, your app sends a message to a central system run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).

NPCI passes the message to your bank, which checks your PIN and balance and takes out the money. It then tells the shop's bank to add the same amount. Both sides get a confirmation, usually within a few seconds. The money goes straight from one [[@money-banks|bank account]] to another.

st.prompt: When you pay with UPI, where is your money kept before you send it?

options.t: In your own bank account
Inside the UPI app on your phone
In a big NPCI account in Mumbai

st.reveal: UPI apps don't hold your money. They pass a message telling your bank to move money straight into the other person's bank account. That is why any UPI app works with any bank.

Your money stays in your bank account the whole time. The app only sends instructions. The money moves straight from your bank to the other person's bank.

sec.t:
UPI launched in 2016. Within a few years it was everywhere, from big malls to [[@street-food|street food]] carts with a laminated QR code taped to the side. Many small sellers who never had [[@nfc-tap|card machines]] started taking digital payments for the first time.

The numbers grew fast. By 2025, people in India were making more than 15 billion UPI payments a month. It became one of the busiest real-time payment systems anywhere.

Cash has not vanished. Many people still prefer notes for small things, and some areas have weak mobile signal. But in big cities, a shopkeeper who can't take UPI is now the unusual one. India also added features such as UPI Lite for tiny payments and ways to pay from basic phones without internet.

UPI also travels. It can be used in places like [[@singapore|Singapore]], the UAE, Nepal and [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], and in 2024 the [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] in Paris began accepting it for tickets.

sec.h: How India and the USA compare
sec.t:
In the United States, people pay with cards and with apps such as Venmo and Zelle. Many of these work well, but for years no single system linked almost every bank and shop with free, instant payments. India built UPI as shared public plumbing that any bank or app could plug into.

Other things India already had helped too. Mobile data was cheap. Hundreds of millions of new bank accounts were opened from 2014 onwards. And [[@aadhaar|Aadhaar]] numbers made it easier for people to prove who they are.

Your UPI PIN is like the key to your bank account. You need it to send money, but never to receive money. Scammers sometimes send a "collect request" or a QR code and say you must enter your PIN to get a prize or refund. That is always a trick.

Banks and NPCI add more checks, such as tying UPI to the SIM card in your phone. The simplest rule still works best: if someone asks for your PIN, say no and tell a trusted adult. Good habits [[@online-safety|online]] matter as much as clever technology.

text: Alexander, a young king from Macedonia in northern Greece, crossed the Hindu Kush mountains into the Indus region in 327–326 BCE. He had already conquered the vast [[@ancient-persia|Persian Empire]]. Some local rulers, such as the king of Taxila, joined him rather than fight.

In 326 BCE he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes river, today's Jhelum, in a hard battle against [[@oddity-elephants-war|war elephants]]. But when his army reached the Beas river, the exhausted soldiers refused to march east. Alexander turned south, sailed down the Indus to the sea and left. He died in Babylon in 323 BCE, aged just 32.

st.prompt: After beating Porus in battle, what did Alexander do with him, according to the Greek writers?

options.t: Let him keep ruling, and even gave him more land
Took him back to Greece as a prisoner
Made him a general in the Greek army

st.reveal: Greek writers say Porus was allowed to keep his kingdom and was given extra territory. Alexander needed loyal local rulers to hold the land behind him as he moved on.

src: Arrian, The Campaigns of Alexander (Anabasis), 2nd century CE.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Alexander the Great.
n.certNote: Almost everything we know comes from Greek and Roman writers, the fullest of whom lived more than 400 years later. Ancient Indian texts do not mention Alexander at all, so details such as army sizes and what Porus said are uncertain.

myth: Alexander conquered India.
Alexander only reached the north-western edge of the subcontinent, in what is now Pakistan and Indian Punjab. He turned back at the Beas river and never saw the Ganga plains.

sec.t:
Porus ruled the land beyond the Jhelum. He lined up his army on the far bank, with elephants in front. Horses panic at the sight and smell of elephants, so Alexander could not simply charge across.

According to the Greek writers, Alexander tricked Porus. For many nights he made noise as if about to cross, until the Indian army stopped reacting. Then, in a [[monsoon|monsoon]] storm, he crossed upstream with part of his army. The battle was fierce. Some elephants, wounded and frightened, trampled soldiers on both sides. Porus, a very tall man on a huge elephant, kept fighting until he was badly wounded.

Alexander wanted to keep going east. He had heard of rich kingdoms on the Ganga, probably the Nanda kingdom of Magadha, with an even larger army and thousands of elephants.

His soldiers had been marching and fighting for about eight years and had travelled thousands of kilometres. The monsoon rains soaked them for weeks. At the Beas river, they refused to cross. After sulking in his tent for three days, Alexander gave in. On the way home, he was badly wounded by an arrow while attacking a town of the Malli people. Later, many of his troops suffered terribly crossing the desert of Gedrosia, in today's Baluchistan.

Indian sources of the time do not mention Alexander at all. To them, he was one of several invaders from the northwest, and he stayed only about two years. His soldiers did not build roads or temples that lasted, and his garrisons soon melted away.

His visit still mattered. Within a few years, a young leader called Chandragupta, guided by his teacher [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], founded the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan Empire]] and took over the northwest. In about 305 BCE, Alexander's general Seleucus made peace with Chandragupta and received 500 elephants in exchange for land. Greek kings ruled parts of Afghanistan and the Punjab for two more centuries. Their art mixed with Indian ideas, and in Gandhara, early Buddhist [[@sculpture|sculptures]] show the Buddha in robes that fall in Greek-style folds.

text: Genghis Khan was a Mongol leader who united the warring tribes of the Mongolian steppe in 1206 and then launched conquests across Asia. He was born with the name Temujin, probably around 1162. "Genghis Khan" was a title, often translated as "universal ruler", though its exact meaning is debated.

By his death in 1227, his armies had conquered northern China, Central Asia and parts of Persia. His sons and grandsons pushed further, creating the largest connected land [[empire|empire]] in history, the [[@mongols|Mongol Empire]]. In Mongolia he is honoured as the founder of the nation. In many places he conquered, he is remembered for terrible destruction.

st.prompt: The Mongols had no writing system before Genghis Khan. What did he do about it?

options.t: Had Mongolian written in the script of the Uyghur people
Ordered everyone to learn Chinese characters
Invented a brand new alphabet himself

st.reveal: Genghis Khan had a captured Uyghur scribe adapt the Uyghur script to write Mongolian. The traditional Mongolian script, written in vertical lines, grew from it and is still used today, especially in Inner Mongolia in China.

src: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th century), translated by Igor de Rachewiltz (Brill, 2004).
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Genghis Khan.
Tatiana Zerjal and others, "The genetic legacy of the Mongols", American Journal of Human Genetics (2003).
n.certNote: The main source for his early life, The Secret History of the Mongols, was written soon after his death and mixes history with legend. His birth year is uncertain, estimated between about 1155 and 1167, and how many people died in his wars is debated.

d.try: Try writing your name in vertical lines, top to bottom, the way traditional Mongolian script is written. Then try writing a short sentence the same way. Does it change how you hold the pen or how fast you write?
myth: Genghis Khan was nothing more than a brutal destroyer.

His wars caused enormous death and destruction. He also created a written script for Mongolian, promoted people by merit, allowed religious freedom and helped connect trade across Asia. Historians try to weigh both sides.

sec.t:
Temujin's father, Yesugei, was a chief. When Temujin was about nine, his father was poisoned by members of a rival tribe, the Tatars. His father's followers then abandoned the family.

Temujin's mother, Hoelun, kept her children alive by gathering wild roots and berries and catching fish and small animals. Life on the steppe was harsh and dangerous. As a teenager Temujin was captured by enemies and escaped. Later his wife, Borte, was kidnapped by another tribe, and he gathered allies to rescue her. Step by step, he built up a band of loyal followers.

The Mongols had no written language. Genghis Khan ordered a captured Uyghur scribe to adapt the Uyghur script for Mongolian. This allowed laws, orders and records to be [[@writing-began|written down]]. The script, written in vertical columns, is still used today.

He also allowed people of different religions to worship freely. Buddhist, Muslim, Christian and Daoist leaders all visited his court. For merchants, he made the roads safer, which helped trade along the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]].

Genghis Khan's armies attacked the Tangut kingdom of Western Xia and the Jin [[dynasty|dynasty]] of northern China, capturing its capital, today's Beijing, in 1215. In 1219 he invaded the Khwarazmian Empire, in Central Asia and Iran, after its governor killed a group of Mongol-sponsored merchants and the shah killed his envoys.

The campaign was devastating. Great cities such as Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv were captured, and many were destroyed. In 1221 he chased the Khwarazmian prince Jalal ad-Din to the Indus river. The prince famously escaped by riding his horse into the river and swimming across. He sought shelter with Sultan Iltutmish of Delhi, who wisely kept his distance. Genghis Khan turned back, and the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] was spared for the time being.

sec.h: A hidden grave and a genetic trail
sec.t:
Genghis Khan died in 1227, during a campaign against the Tanguts. How he died is unclear. He was buried in a secret place, probably in the Khentii mountains of Mongolia, and the location has never been found.

In 2003, geneticists found that about 8 per cent of men in a large region of Asia carry a very similar Y [[chromosome|chromosome]], the part of [[@dna|DNA]] passed from father to son. They suggested it might come from Genghis Khan and his male relatives. Other scientists think the evidence is not strong enough to name him. Today his face appears on Mongolian banknotes, and Ulaanbaatar's international airport bears his name.

text: Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan scholar who travelled further than almost anyone before modern times. Over about 29 years, he covered roughly 1,20,000 km, by many estimates, three times around the Earth's [[equator|equator]].

He left Tangier in 1325 to make the hajj, the [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] to Mecca. Then he kept going. He crossed North Africa, Arabia, Persia and Central Asia, worked in [[@delhi|Delhi]], lived in the [[@maldives|Maldives]], visited [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]] and reached China. Later he travelled to Spain and across the [[@sahara|Sahara]] to the [[@ancient-africa|empire of Mali]]. Back home, he told his story to a scholar, and the result was a book called the *Rihla*, which is still read today.

He kept a diary every day for 29 years

st.reveal: In about 1355, the Sultan of Morocco asked a young scholar named Ibn Juzayy to write down Ibn Battuta's memories. Ibn Battuta had lost many of his notes in shipwrecks and robberies, so much of the book came from memory.

n.certNote: Most of Ibn Battuta's account matches other records and is trusted. Some parts, such as his trip to China, have puzzled historians, and he may have borrowed a few descriptions from other writers.

myth: Medieval Muslims rarely travelled beyond their homelands.
Pilgrims, scholars and traders travelled widely across Africa, Asia and Europe. Ibn Battuta found Muslim communities, mosques and fellow travellers almost everywhere he went.

sec.t:
Ibn Battuta was 21 when he set out, travelling alone at first. He later wrote that leaving his parents was as painful for him as it was for them. He joined [[caravan|caravans]] for safety, and in Egypt a holy man told him he would visit faraway lands.

After reaching Mecca, he decided to see as much of the Muslim world as he could, and to never take the same road twice if he could help it. He trained as a judge in Islamic law, and that skill let him find work and respect wherever there were Muslim rulers.

The journey to China went wrong from the start. In Calicut, in [[@kerala|Kerala]], the ships were wrecked in a storm, and Ibn Battuta lost almost everything. Afraid to go back to Delhi, he sailed to the Maldives.

There he became a judge again and married. He found the islands beautiful, and noted that their money was cowrie shells. After less than a year, he left for Sri Lanka, where he climbed Adam's Peak, a mountain holy to Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims and Christians.

Eventually he reached China by sea. He admired its silk, its porcelain and its paper money, and wrote that a traveller could journey safely there even with lots of goods. Historians are unsure how far inside China he really went.

Heading home, he passed through Damascus in 1348 during the [[@black-death|Black Death]], a plague that killed huge numbers of people. He reached [[@morocco|Morocco]] in 1349 to find that his mother had died of it months earlier.

Ibn Battuta still wasn't finished. He visited Muslim Spain, then crossed the Sahara with a camel caravan in 1352 to the [[empire|empire]] of Mali, where he saw Timbuktu.

The Sultan of Morocco then asked him to share his adventures. A scholar named Ibn Juzayy wrote them down in 1355. Ibn Battuta died around 1368 or 1369. Today a large shopping mall in [[@dubai|Dubai]] is named after him, with sections designed in the styles of the lands he visited.

text: Rosa Parks was a Black woman from Montgomery, Alabama. On 1 December 1955 she refused a bus driver's order to give up her seat to a white passenger, and she was arrested.

At the time, Montgomery's laws kept Black and white passengers apart on buses. Her arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. For more than a year, Black residents refused to ride the city's buses. In 1956, the US [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] agreed that bus segregation was against [[@us-constitution|the Constitution]], and the boycott ended in victory. Parks became known as "the mother of the civil rights movement".

The city put on free trains

st.reveal: Many people walked kilometres each day. Others used a network of more than 200 volunteer cars, with pick-up points around the city. Some Black taxi drivers charged bus-fare prices to help.

She wrote later that the only tired she was, was tired of giving in. She was an experienced activist who had worked for years with the civil rights group NAACP.

sec.t:
In Montgomery, the front seats of each bus were kept for white passengers. Black passengers, who made up most of the riders, sat at the back. The middle rows were in between. If the white section filled up, the driver could order Black passengers in the middle to stand.

Black passengers often had to pay at the front, get off, and walk around to enter through the back door. Sometimes the bus drove off before they got back on.

Parks worked as a seamstress, sewing and altering clothes at a department store. That evening she boarded the bus home and sat in the first row of the middle section. When more white passengers got on, the driver told her row to move. Three people stood up. Parks did not.

The driver called the police, and she was arrested. She was later fined 10 dollars, plus 4 dollars in court costs.

Parks was calm and polite, but her choice was not random. She had been secretary of the local branch of the NAACP, a civil rights group, since 1943. That summer she had attended a training centre for activists in Tennessee.

She had also been thrown off a bus by the same driver, James Blake, twelve years earlier, in 1943.

She was not the first to refuse. Nine months earlier, a 15-year-old named [[@people-kids-changemakers|Claudette Colvin]] had done the same thing on a Montgomery bus. Leaders felt Parks, a respected and well-known member of the community, would be the right person to rally around.

Within days, Black leaders called a boycott and chose a young minister, [[@martin-luther-king|Martin Luther King Jr.]], to lead it. Black residents walked, shared rides and used church-organised cars. The bus company lost most of its passengers.

The boycott held through a year of threats and arrests. In November 1956, the Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was illegal. The boycott ended on 20 December 1956.

Parks paid a price. She lost her job, received threats and in 1957 moved with her husband to Detroit. There she worked for many years in the office of a US congressman, John Conyers.

She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1996 and the Congressional Gold Medal in 1999. When she died in 2005, she became the first woman to lie in honour in the US Capitol building.

{{story:museums}}

The bus itself was found rusting in a field and was bought in 2001 by The Henry Ford, a [[@museums|museum]] in Dearborn, Michigan. After careful restoration, it sits in the museum today. Visitors can climb aboard and sit in the row where she refused to stand.

text: Making a book takes many people and many months. A writer writes it. Editors help improve it and check it. Designers choose the size, fonts and cover. Then the files go to a printer, who prints the pages on huge sheets of paper, folds them into bundles, binds them together and trims the edges.
A typical paperback might take a year or more from finished [[manuscript|manuscript]] to bookshop. The printing itself can take only a few hours, even for thousands of copies.

sec.t:
A book starts as a manuscript, the writer's version. An editor reads it and suggests changes: cut this chapter, explain that idea, make this character braver. The writer revises. Then a copy-editor checks spelling, [[@grammar-why|grammar]], facts and consistency, like whether a character's eyes stay brown all the way through.

A designer lays out the pages. They choose a typeface, decide how wide the margins are and where pictures go. A [[@picture-books|picture book]] may be designed spread by spread, with the illustrator and designer working together. The pages are checked again as "proofs" to catch any last mistakes.

Every published book also gets an ISBN, an International Standard Book Number. Since 2007 it has had 13 digits, and the last one is a check digit worked out from the others. It is usually printed under a [[@barcodes|barcode]] on the back cover.

Most books are printed by offset lithography. The page images are put on thin metal plates. Oily [[@ink|ink]] sticks to the image areas, and water keeps the blank areas clean. The ink passes from the plate to a rubber blanket and then onto the paper.

The paper is much bigger than a single page. One sheet might carry 16 or 32 pages, arranged in a pattern called an imposition. Some pages are upside down and in a strange order, so they end up correct once the sheet is folded.

This idea goes back to the early days of the [[@printing-press|printing press]]. [[@printing-revolution|Johannes Gutenberg]]'s workshop in Germany printed its famous Bible in the 1450s, with more than one page on each sheet.

{{story:printing-press}}

A machine folds each printed sheet into a bundle called a signature. The signatures are stacked in order, which is called gathering. Look at the top or bottom edge of a thick hardback and you can often see the separate bundles.

For a sewn binding, threads stitch through the fold of each signature and hold them together. This lets the book open flat and last a long time. Many paperbacks are "perfect bound" instead: the folds are trimmed off and the loose pages are [[@glue-sticky|glued]] at the spine.

Then a big blade trims three edges so the pages can be turned. Hardbacks get stiff boards covered in cloth or paper, and sometimes a separate paper jacket.

The [[@paper-made|paper]] for most books comes from wood pulp, and many publishers now use paper from forests certified as well managed. Some books are printed in India and the US for local readers. Others are printed in one country and shipped around the world.

Once printed, a book goes to warehouses, shops and [[@libraries|libraries]]. Many are also turned into e-books and audiobooks. But the folded sheet has survived since the 1400s, because it works. Hold a book up to the light at the spine and you can still see the trace of every fold.

text: Africa has an enormous treasure of folk tales, told for thousands of years in more than 2,000 languages. Many were never written down until recently. Instead, they were spoken, sung and acted out, passed from grandparents to children around fires and in village squares.

Some characters appear again and again. There's Anansi, a crafty spider from the Akan people of Ghana. There's Tortoise, a sly schemer in Yoruba and Igbo stories from Nigeria, and Hare, a quick-witted trickster across East and Southern Africa. There are also grand epics about real kings, like Sundiata, who founded the [[@mali-empire|Mali Empire]] about 800 years ago.

st.reveal: Anansi struggles to climb with the pot tied to his front. His young son suggests tying it to his back. Furious that a child is smarter than him, Anansi drops the pot, and wisdom spreads all over the world.

sec.t:
In one tale from Ghana, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the sky god. Anansi asked to buy them. Nyame laughed and set a price no one could pay: bring me a python, a leopard, a swarm of hornets and a fairy who can't be seen.

Anansi tricked each one. He fooled the python into stretching along a pole to "measure" himself, then tied him up. He trapped the leopard in a pit and caught the hornets by pretending it was raining. Nyame kept his word. Ever since, Akan stories are often called *anansesem*, "spider stories", even when Anansi isn't in them. Real [[@spiders-silk|spiders]] aren't quite so cunning, but they are clever builders.

In West Africa, especially in Mali, Guinea, Senegal and Gambia, families of [[griot|griots]] have kept history alive for centuries. A griot is a storyteller, singer and historian. Many play the kora, a harp-like instrument with 21 strings.

Griots tell the epic of Sundiata, a prince who couldn't walk as a child and was mocked for it. One day he pulled himself up using an iron bar, grew strong and later defeated a cruel sorcerer-king to found the Mali Empire. Griots still perform the epic today, and some versions take many hours to tell.

From the 1500s to the 1800s, millions of Africans were captured and taken as enslaved people to the Americas. They were forced to leave almost everything behind, but they kept their stories. Anansi became "Anancy" in Jamaica and "Aunt Nancy" in parts of the southern USA. The African hare grew into Brer Rabbit, the small trickster who outsmarts bigger animals.

These [[trickster|trickster]] tales mattered. A small creature beating a powerful one with brains was a story of hope.

sec.h: Why the sky is far away
sec.t:
Many African stories explain how the world got its shape. In one, told in Nigeria, the sky once hung so low that people tore off pieces to eat. The sky warned them not to waste it, but people grew greedy, so it rose up high out of reach.

African tales are also loved worldwide in picture books. In 1976 *Why Mosquitoes Buzz in People's Ears*, a West African tale retold by Verna Aardema, won America's top award for illustration, the Caldecott Medal. And the strangest part? Trickster animals and talking-animal lessons turn up in India too, in the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], and in Greece, in the fables of [[@aesop|Aesop]].
